summary: This standards-track memo defines the procedures for using the Kerberos V5 mechanism with the GSS-API. It updates RFC 1964 with incremental changes in response to developments since that document.

eli5.summary: Programs wanting security can use a common doorway, GSS-API. This document says how Kerberos plugs into that doorway.

questions: what is a gss-api mic token
what is the rrc field in a wrap token
subtitle: How Kerberos 5 plugs into the GSS-API, with new message-protection tokens that work with any Kerberos cipher.

tldr.problem: The original Kerberos GSS-API mechanism in RFC 1964 put an algorithm identifier in every protected message, which does not fit the newer Kerberos cryptosystem framework that allows new ciphers and checksums.
tldr.mechanism: Per-message tokens drop the algorithm identifiers and instead use the cipher and required checksum of the session key or subkey, with directional key derivation, a 64-bit sequence number and new MIC and Wrap token layouts.
tldr.outcome: The new token formats MUST be used with all newer encryption types, and the RFC updates RFC 1964; later RFCs have in turn updated this one.

today: RFC 4121 is a Proposed Standard that updates RFC 1964, and it has itself been updated by RFC 5896, RFC 6112, RFC 6542, RFC 6649 and RFC 8062.

sections.title: Why Version 2 of the Mechanism
sections.content:
RFC 1964 defined the Kerberos Version 5 mechanism for the GSS-API: the formats of context establishment, per-message and context deletion tokens, with an algorithm identifier for each cryptosystem in the per-message and deletion tokens. RFC 3961 later defined a generic framework for Kerberos encryption and checksum types.

RFC 4121 obviates the algorithm identifiers. Per-message tokens use the encryption algorithm given by the crypto profile of the session key or subkey made during context negotiation, along with its required checksum algorithm. Token layouts lose their algorithm indicators and gain extra information for the generic framework.

The new token formats MUST be used with all "newer" encryption types, meaning those specified with or since RFC 3961. They MAY be used with other types if both sides know from context establishment that they can process them. The data exchanged with the Key Distribution Center is not specific to GSS-API and stays defined in RFC 4120.
sections.eli5: The old way stuck a label on every message saying which lock was used. The new way just uses whatever lock the two sides already agreed on, so no label is needed.

sections.title: Keys and Quality of Protection
sections.content:
To limit how much any one key is exposed, RFC 3961 derives separate keys for separate purposes from a base key. This RFC defines four key usage values for deriving the signing and sealing keys from the session key or subkey made during context establishment. The sender's role (acceptor or initiator) and the token type (MIC or Wrap) pick the value. The Wrap values are used even when the Wrap token gives no confidentiality.

The base key is chosen in order. If the acceptor asserts a subkey in the AP-REP message, that is used, and later per-message tokens MUST carry the AcceptorSubkey flag. Otherwise, if the initiator asserts a subkey in the AP-REQ message, that is used. Otherwise it is the session key in the service ticket.

The GSS-API Quality of Protection (QOP) value lets applications ask for a type of protection. With these tokens the algorithms follow from the key, so the QOP value is ignored.
sections.eli5: Instead of using one key for everything, each direction and each job gets its own key made from a master key. The sender and the receiver pick the master key in a fixed order.

sections.title: Context Establishment Tokens
sections.content:
Context establishment tokens use the generic GSS-API framing from RFC 2743. Inside, the innerToken starts with a two-octet TOK_ID in big-endian order, followed by a Kerberos message: KRB_AP_REQ (01 00), KRB_AP_REP (02 00) or KRB_ERROR (03 00). If an unknown TOK_ID arrives in the first token, the receiver MUST return GSS_S_CONTINUE_NEEDED and its output token MUST contain a KRB_ERROR with the code KRB_AP_ERR_MSG_TYPE.

The authenticator in the KRB_AP_REQ MUST include the optional sequence number and the checksum field, which carries service flags, channel bindings and optional delegation information. The checksum type MUST be 0x8003. Its layout is: Lgth (octets 0 to 3, the value 16 in little-endian order), Bnd (octets 4 to 19, channel binding information), Flags (octets 20 to 23), and, only when GSS_C_DELEG_FLAG is set, DlgOpt, Dlgth and Deleg, which holds a KRB_CRED message carrying a ticket-granting ticket. Optional Exts follow.

The defined flags are GSS_C_DELEG_FLAG (1), GSS_C_MUTUAL_FLAG (2), GSS_C_REPLAY_FLAG (4), GSS_C_SEQUENCE_FLAG (8), GSS_C_CONF_FLAG (16) and GSS_C_INTEG_FLAG (32). Undefined flags MUST be cleared by the sender and unknown flags MUST be ignored by the receiver.

The Bnd field is the MD5 hash of the channel bindings, taken over all non-null components in order of declaration, or 16 zero-valued octets when the caller passes GSS_C_NO_BINDINGS. Context deletion tokens are empty: both peers call GSS_Delete_sec_context() independently.
sections.eli5: Setting up a secure chat starts with a hello message that carries a small form: which services are wanted and which connection it is meant for. Closing the chat needs no message at all, since each side just throws away its own notes.

sections.title: MIC and Wrap Tokens
sections.content:
Once the context exists, two token classes protect individual messages. A MIC token, from GSS_GetMIC(), travels separately from the data and lets the receiver verify its integrity. A Wrap token, from GSS_Wrap(), carries the data itself, either encrypted or in plaintext followed by a checksum. These tokens do not use the generic GSS-API framing.

Shared header fields: TOK_ID (04 04 for MIC, 05 04 for Wrap), a one-octet Flags field and an 8-octet SND_SEQ sequence number, a 64-bit big-endian integer that rises by one after each token to tell intentional repeats from replays. The flag bits are SentByAcceptor (bit 0), Sealed (bit 1, Wrap only) and AcceptorSubkey (bit 2). The direction bit stops an adversary from reflecting a message back.

A Wrap token also has the EC field (the filler length with confidentiality, or the trailing checksum length without) and the RRC right rotation count. RRC lets existing SSPI applications encrypt in place: the token after the first 16 octets is rotated right by RRC octets, and receivers MUST handle every rotation count, including ones larger than the token.

With confidentiality, the token is the header followed by the encryption of the plaintext, filler and a copy of the header, with RRC zeroed in the encrypted copy. Without it, a checksum is computed over the data and then the header, with EC and RRC zeroed, and appended. MIC checksums cover the data and then octets 0 to 15. Either way the data is bound to the header, including the sequence number and direction.
sections.eli5: Each protected message wears a small label with a counter and a direction mark, so a copied or reversed message gets caught. The message is then either locked in a box or sent open with a tamper seal.

sections.title: Limits and Backwards Compatibility
sections.content:
The new token formats are only recognized by new implementations. For keys of types that are not "newer", implementations can always fall back to the sign or seal algorithms of RFC 1964. Retrying a message in the old format would need a secure negotiation mechanism such as RFC 2478 or an out-of-band choice, so the RFC recommends using the new formats only when both peers are known to support them, for example because of new encryption types.

To tell formats apart, a receiver checks the first octet of a token: 0x60 means the generic GSS-API framing; otherwise the first two octets are the TOK_ID. Identifiers 0x60 0x00 through 0x60 0xFF are reserved and SHALL NOT be assigned, so this check is unambiguous.

All implementations MUST accept buffers of at least 16K octets for GSS_GetMIC(), GSS_VerifyMIC() and GSS_Wrap(), and the output of a Wrap of 16K octets must be accepted by GSS_Unwrap(). They SHOULD support 64K octet buffers. The RFC also recommends symbolic names for minor status codes, such as GSS_KRB5_S_KG_NO_SUBKEY.
sections.eli5: New and old versions have to get along. The first byte of a message says which style it is, and both sides should only use the new style when they know the other side can read it.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
Channel bindings are checked by the acceptor. The acceptor can ignore the initiator's channel bindings if the application does not use them in GSS_Accept_sec_context and the acceptor does not prove to the initiator that it has the same bindings, even if the client asked for mutual authentication. Application designers who rely on channel bindings should keep this limit in mind.

The KDC selects session key types, and this mechanism has no negotiation of algorithms, so an acceptor cannot ask clients to avoid types it does not understand. Administrators can restrict the session key types the KDC will use for a service. The catch is a service name used for both GSS-API and non-GSS-API traffic: if the GSS-API software does not support a cipher such as AES but the Kerberos software does, AES keys cannot be issued for it, which keeps the non-GSS-API services weaker than necessary. Administrators should weigh that loss of protection against interoperability.
sections.eli5: The server cannot tell clients which locks it can open, because the key office picks the lock. Forcing old locks everywhere keeps things working but makes everything easier to break.
